questions.stem: International trade takes place mainly because:
options: governments require every country to trade a set amount each year
one country must always lose so that the other country can gain
countries cannot produce any goods or services for themselves
both trading partners expect to gain from voluntary exchange
questions.explanation: Trade is voluntary, so it occurs only when both sides expect to be better off. It is not a zero-sum game in which one side's gain is the other's loss.

questions.stem: International trade improves the allocation of resources mainly because it:
options: lets each country specialise in what it makes most efficiently
requires every country to produce all of the goods it consumes
keeps resources in industries that cannot compete with imports
prevents consumers from buying goods made in other countries
questions.explanation: Specialisation moves resources into the uses where they are most productive, raising total output. Keeping resources in uncompetitive industries wastes them.

questions.stem: Australia exports large amounts of iron ore and imports most of its passenger cars. The main basis for this pattern of trade is that:
options: car-producing countries are not permitted to mine their own iron ore deposits
Australian consumers prefer imported goods to Australian goods in every case
Australia has abundant minerals and relatively high manufacturing costs
Australia has no manufacturing industry of any kind and so cannot make goods
questions.explanation: Differences in resource endowments and costs mean Australia produces minerals relatively cheaply and buys cars from countries with large-scale car industries. Australia still has manufacturing, though not mass car production.

questions.stem: Australia's largest two-way trading partner is:
options: China
the United States
the United Kingdom
New Zealand
questions.explanation: China has been Australia's largest trading partner since 2007, buying large volumes of iron ore, coal and gas. The United States is the next largest two-way trading partner.

questions.stem: Which is Australia's largest goods export by value?
options: Wool
Iron ore
Wheat
Passenger cars
questions.explanation: Iron ore, used in steelmaking, has been Australia's largest export for many years, followed by other resources such as coal and natural gas. Wool and wheat were once dominant but are now much smaller.

questions.stem: The composition of Australia's trade refers to:
options: the difference between the value of exports and imports
the types of goods and services Australia trades
the countries that Australia exports to and imports from
the total dollar value of Australia's exports and imports
questions.explanation: Composition is what is traded, such as resources, manufactures and services. Direction is who Australia trades with, and value is the dollar amount.

questions.stem: The direction of Australia's trade over recent decades has shifted mainly:
options: towards South America, especially Brazil and Argentina
towards Africa, especially South Africa and Nigeria
towards Asia, especially China, Japan, South Korea and India
towards Europe, especially the United Kingdom and Germany
questions.explanation: Rapid growth in Asian economies has made the region Australia's main market, replacing the United Kingdom, which dominated trade until the mid-twentieth century.

questions.stem: Which is Australia's largest services export?
options: Film and television productions sold abroad
Education-related travel by international students
Financial services sold to overseas banks
Construction services for overseas projects
questions.explanation: Spending by international students on fees and living costs is recorded as a services export and is Australia's largest services export. Tourism is another major services export.

questions.stem: Which list best describes the composition of Australia's imports?
options: Mainly agricultural products such as wheat, wool and beef
Mainly services such as education provided to international students
Mainly manufactured goods such as refined fuels, vehicles and electronics
Mainly raw minerals such as iron ore, coal and natural gas
questions.explanation: Australia imports refined fuels, passenger cars, telecommunications equipment and other manufactures, along with services such as overseas travel. Minerals and farm products are mainly exported.

questions.stem: When the value of a country's exports exceeds the value of its imports, it has:
options: balanced trade
a budget surplus
a trade surplus
a trade deficit
questions.explanation: A trade surplus means more is earned from selling goods and services overseas than is spent on imports. A budget surplus refers to government revenue exceeding spending.

questions.stem: In a quarter, Australia's exports of goods and services were $160 billion and imports were $148 billion. The trade outcome was:
options: a deficit of $12 billion
a surplus of $308 billion
balanced trade
a surplus of $12 billion
questions.explanation: Balance on goods and services = exports - imports = 160 - 148 = +$12 billion, a surplus. Adding the two figures gives total trade, not the balance.

questions.stem: World prices for iron ore and coal fall sharply while import spending is unchanged. Australia's trade balance is most likely to:
options: move towards deficit, as export earnings fall
move towards surplus, as export earnings rise
move towards surplus, as import spending falls
stay the same, because export volumes are unchanged
questions.explanation: With commodities dominating exports, lower prices cut the value of exports even if volumes hold, so the balance worsens. Imports are unchanged in this scenario.

questions.stem: Balanced trade occurs when:
options: the volume of exports equals the volume of imports
exports and imports both grow by the same percentage
the country trades equally with every partner country
the value of exports equals the value of imports
questions.explanation: Trade balance is measured in value: when export earnings equal import spending, the balance is zero. Equal volumes do not mean equal values, because prices differ.

questions.stem: Foreign debt is best described as:
options: foreign ownership of shares in Australian companies and property
the value of goods imported from overseas but not yet paid for
Australian Government spending on foreign aid programs
money borrowed from overseas that must be repaid with interest
questions.explanation: Debt creates an obligation to pay interest and repay the principal. Ownership of shares is foreign equity, which pays dividends from profits rather than interest.

questions.stem: A Japanese company buys a large share of an Australian gas company. This adds to:
options: foreign debt owed by Australia
Australia's equity abroad
Australia's exports of goods
foreign equity in Australia
questions.explanation: Purchases of shares and other ownership stakes by foreigners are foreign equity investment. If the Japanese company had instead lent money to the Australian firm, it would add to foreign debt.

questions.stem: An Australian bank borrows $US5 billion from investors in the United States. This transaction increases:
options: Australia's equity abroad
Australia's export income
Australia's foreign debt
foreign equity in Australia
questions.explanation: Borrowing from overseas lenders adds to foreign debt, which must be serviced with interest. Australian banks have long raised part of their funding offshore.

questions.stem: Which is a key difference between foreign debt and foreign equity for Australia?
options: Debt must be serviced regardless of profits, while equity returns depend on profits
Equity must be serviced regardless of profits, while debt returns depend on profits
Debt gives foreign lenders ownership and voting rights in Australian companies
Equity must always be repaid in full within a fixed period, unlike debt
questions.explanation: Interest on debt must be paid even when businesses struggle, while dividends to foreign shareholders fall when profits fall. Equity gives ownership; debt does not.

questions.stem: Australia has historically relied on foreign investment mainly because:
options: foreign investment is the only way for Australia to buy imports
national saving has been too low to fund all its investment opportunities
Australian households save more than businesses could ever invest
the government requires all new businesses to be foreign-owned
questions.explanation: Australia has had more profitable investment opportunities, especially in resources, than domestic saving could fund, so foreign capital has filled the gap. Compulsory superannuation has since raised national saving.

questions.stem: Which country is the largest source of foreign investment in Australia?
options: China
New Zealand
Saudi Arabia
The United States
questions.explanation: The United States is by far the largest investor in Australia and also the largest destination for Australian investment abroad. China is the largest trading partner but a much smaller investor.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit to Australia of foreign investment?
options: It reduces interest payments that Australia makes to the rest of the world
It funds investment that raises production, jobs and exports
It guarantees that all profits remain within the Australian economy
It removes the need for Australians to save for the future
questions.explanation: Foreign capital has financed mines, gas projects and infrastructure that domestic saving could not fully fund. A cost is the flow of interest and dividends to overseas investors.

questions.stem: A cost of high foreign debt is that it:
options: prevents Australian businesses from investing in new capital equipment
reduces the interest payments that must be made to overseas lenders
leaves the economy exposed if overseas lenders raise rates or pull out
gives foreign lenders ownership and control of Australian businesses
questions.explanation: Debt must be refinanced and serviced, so a rise in global interest rates or a loss of lender confidence can sharply raise costs. Ownership and control come with equity, not debt.

questions.stem: An exchange rate is:
options: the interest rate charged on loans between banks in different countries
the rate at which a country's exports grow compared with its imports
the rate of tax charged on goods that cross a country's border
the price of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
questions.explanation: For example, $A1 = $US0.65 means one Australian dollar buys 65 US cents. A tax on imports is a tariff.

questions.stem: Exchange rates are needed for international trade and investment because:
options: buyers and sellers in different countries usually use different currencies
every country uses the same currency, so prices must be converted for tax
exchange rates set the quantity of goods each country may export
exchange rates determine the interest rate on all foreign loans
questions.explanation: A Japanese steelmaker paying for Australian iron ore must obtain Australian dollars, so currencies must be exchanged. The exchange rate sets how much of one currency is needed to buy another.

questions.stem: A bilateral exchange rate measures the value of the Australian dollar against:
options: the price of gold, set daily by the world's central banks
the inflation rate in Australia compared with other countries
one other currency, such as the US dollar or the Japanese yen
a weighted basket of the currencies of all major trading partners
questions.explanation: Bilateral means two-way: $A1 = $US0.65 or $A1 = 98 yen. The trade-weighted index measures the dollar against a basket of currencies.

questions.stem: The exchange rate is $A1 = $US0.70. How many US dollars would an Australian tourist receive for $A2,000?
questions.explanation: US dollars = Australian dollars x 0.70 = 2,000 x 0.70 = $US1,400. Dividing by 0.70 gives $US2,857, which converts in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: The exchange rate is $A1 = 100 Japanese yen. A Japanese buyer wants to buy Australian beef priced at $A30 a kilogram. The price in yen is:
options: 130 yen a kilogram
3,000 yen a kilogram
0.30 yen a kilogram
300 yen a kilogram
questions.explanation: Yen price = $A30 x 100 = 3,000 yen. If the dollar rose to 110 yen, the same beef would cost 3,300 yen, making it less competitive in Japan.

questions.stem: The exchange rate moves from $A1 = $US0.62 to $A1 = $US0.68. The Australian dollar has:
options: depreciated, so exports to the US become dearer
appreciated, so imports from the US become cheaper
depreciated, so imports from the US become cheaper
appreciated, so imports from the US become dearer
questions.explanation: Each Australian dollar now buys more US dollars, an appreciation, so US goods cost fewer Australian dollars. Australian exports become dearer for US buyers.

questions.stem: The Australian dollar rises against the US dollar but falls against the Japanese yen. Which statement is correct?
options: Imports from the US become cheaper while imports from Japan become dearer
Imports from both the US and Japan become cheaper for Australian buyers
Imports from the US become dearer while imports from Japan become cheaper
Imports from both the US and Japan become dearer for Australian buyers
questions.explanation: Bilateral rates can move in different directions at once. A stronger dollar against the US dollar cheapens US goods, while a weaker dollar against the yen makes Japanese goods dearer.

questions.stem: The balance of payments is:
options: a record of the total value of goods and services produced in Australia
a record of all transactions between Australian residents and the rest of the world
a record of all government revenue and spending over a financial year
a record of all money borrowed and lent between Australian banks
questions.explanation: The balance of payments records trade, income flows and investment flows between Australia and other countries over a period. Government revenue and spending are recorded in the Budget.

questions.stem: The balance of payments has two main accounts. They are the:
options: debt account and the equity account
current account and the capital and financial account
recurrent account and the non-recurrent account
private sector account and the public sector account
questions.explanation: The current account records trade in goods and services and income flows; the capital and financial account records investment flows such as borrowing and share purchases. Recurrent and non-recurrent describe government spending.

questions.stem: Which transaction is recorded in the current account of the balance of payments?
options: A US fund's purchase of shares in an Australian bank
An Australian company borrowing from a Japanese lender
A Chinese firm buying a stake in an Australian mine
An Australian winery selling wine to a buyer in Singapore
questions.explanation: Exports of goods are part of the current account. Purchases of shares, borrowing and buying ownership stakes are investment flows recorded in the capital and financial account.

questions.stem: A main purpose of the balance of payments is to:
options: show how a country's international transactions are financed
set the exchange rate that the Reserve Bank must maintain against other currencies
determine the amount of tax that importers and exporters must pay each year
record the value of goods and services produced within the country each year
questions.explanation: The balance of payments shows whether a country is earning or spending more internationally and how the gap is financed by investment flows. It helps policymakers assess external vulnerability.

questions.stem: Australia buys more goods, services and income from the world than it sells. The balance of payments shows this gap must be matched by:
options: a fall in the exchange rate that fully eliminates the gap
a net inflow of foreign investment in the capital and financial account
a net outflow of foreign investment in the capital and financial account
a surplus in the government's Budget for the same financial year
questions.explanation: A current account deficit is financed by borrowing from or selling assets to foreigners, a net capital inflow. In principle the two accounts sum to zero.

questions.stem: Interest paid by an Australian company to overseas lenders appears in the balance of payments as:
options: a credit in the financial account
a debit in the current account
a credit in the current account
an import of goods
questions.explanation: Payments of interest and dividends to foreigners are income outflows, recorded as debits in the current account (primary income). Persistent debits like this are linked to foreign debt and equity.

questions.stem: Which of these is an Australian export of a service?
options: An Australian retailer buying clothing made in Vietnam
An Australian farmer selling wheat to a buyer in Egypt
A German tourist spending money on a holiday in Queensland
An Australian family spending money on a holiday in Bali
questions.explanation: Spending by overseas visitors in Australia brings in foreign income for services, so it counts as an export. Australians holidaying overseas are importing services, and wheat is a goods export.

questions.stem: An Australian exporter sells machinery to the US for $US65,000. The exchange rate moves from $A1 = $US0.65 to $A1 = $US0.80 before payment is converted. The exporter's revenue in Australian dollars:
options: rises from $A100,000 to $A123,077
falls from $A100,000 to $A52,000
stays at $A100,000, as the US price is fixed
falls from $A100,000 to $A81,250
questions.explanation: At 0.65 the sale is worth 65,000 / 0.65 = $A100,000; at 0.80 it is worth 65,000 / 0.80 = $A81,250. An appreciating dollar reduces the Australian dollar value of foreign-currency export earnings.

questions.stem: Australia's exports are dominated by a few commodities sold mainly to Asian markets. The main risk this composition and direction of trade creates is that:
options: a slowdown in Asian demand or a fall in commodity prices sharply cuts export income
Australian exporters cannot sell to Asian markets because of distance and transport costs
Australia's imports must also come entirely from Asia, raising their prices for consumers
the value of Australia's exports can never change once the trade agreements are signed
questions.explanation: Concentration on a few products and markets means shocks to commodity prices or to growth in China and the region feed quickly into Australia's export income. Diversifying products and markets spreads the risk.
